title: Testing Instructions for a Laboratory Task
transcript:
I've read your proposal for testing the new laboratory instructions. You want to compare a written sheet with a version that includes diagrams. What do you expect the diagrams to change?
I thought students would finish the task more quickly. The task is assembling a simple filter, and the written sheet describes each part separately. A picture might make the relationship between the parts easier to understand.
That is a reasonable starting point, but speed alone may not tell us whether the instructions are better. Someone could finish quickly by skipping a step. What else could you record while they work?
We could count errors, especially when students connect pieces in the wrong order. I'd also like to use a checklist so the observer records the same things for every participant, rather than writing general impressions.
Good. Who will take part? Your draft mentions recruiting from the advanced chemistry class, but those students may already know the equipment. Their previous knowledge could hide differences between the two instruction formats.
Then we should recruit beginners from another introductory science course. We can ask about prior experience before assigning them to groups. Anyone who has already completed this exact task could be excluded from the comparison.
Yes, and distribute the remaining participants randomly. Another issue is the observer. If you help when someone looks confused, you may unintentionally give one group more support. How could you reduce that problem?
The observer could read a fixed response whenever someone asks for help. We should explain that rule beforehand, so it doesn't seem unfriendly. I can include a brief practice session using unrelated equipment before the actual task.
That would help people understand the procedure. Make sure the practice doesn't teach the assembly skill you intend to measure. What will happen after the task, once the timing and error records are complete?
We will conduct short interviews. I want to ask which instruction was hardest to interpret, rather than whether they liked the sheet overall. A positive opinion wouldn't necessarily explain what caused a mistake.
Exactly. Your report should connect those comments to observed behaviour without treating every comment as a reliable explanation. Participants sometimes reconstruct their reasoning after an event, especially when they know they have made an error.
I'll revise the proposal to include both completion time and errors, and separate those results from the interview comments. We can then judge whether diagrams improve performance, instead of assuming that an attractive page must be more effective.

questions.prompt: Why is completion time insufficient as the only measure?
options: Students might finish quickly by omitting steps
The task has no clear finishing point
questions.answer: Students might finish quickly by omitting steps
questions.explanation: 导师指出漏步骤也可能导致快速完成。

questions.prompt: Observers will use a ____ to record the same actions.
questions.explanation: 统一清单使不同参与者的行为记录可比较。

questions.prompt: The study should recruit ____ rather than advanced chemistry students.
questions.explanation: 初学者不熟悉设备，更能显示说明格式的差异。

questions.prompt: After the task, participants will take part in short ____.
questions.explanation: 任务后安排简短访谈，询问难懂的步骤。

questions.prompt: What does the tutor warn about interview comments?
options: They may be explanations constructed afterwards
They always reveal the exact cause of an error
questions.answer: They may be explanations constructed afterwards
questions.explanation: 参与者可能事后重构理由，不能将每条评论直接视为可靠原因。
